text: For 60 years, every textbook, every documentary, every museum diorama told you the exact same story. Man-hunted, woman-gathered. Simple, clean, biology. That story was invented in one room, in one year, by 70 men who never once dug up a single bone to check if it was true. And when scientists finally did check the bones, the whole thing fell apart. Here's something they never tell you. The idea of Man the Hunter is an ancient wisdom passed down through science. It has a literal birth certificate. It was born at a 1966 symposium at the University of Chicago called, you guessed it, Man the Hunter. Damn. Now they are using cartoons to paint men in a bad light. This cartoon basically conveys the idea that for 60 years, every information about hunter-gatherer societies told us that only men hunted, and only women gathered. And that this myth was invented in 1966 by a room full of male anthropologists. First of all, very few, if any, sources, researchers, and studies claim that only men hunted, and only women gathered. Even in the 1966 conference that he mentioned, it was noted that women sometimes hunted. So it seems like it has never really been in dispute among specialists. There could be certain bias, for sure, but normally, the claim is that men generally hunted more, especially large game, while women generally gathered more. The absolute version is something the author of this video invented, so that he could knock it down, push his narrative, and paint men in a bad light. So it was never 100% men hunting and 100% women gathering. Women sometimes hunted. Men also gathered, helped with child care, and performed many other tasks. The exact division varied between different societies and environments. Second of all, anthropologists did not suddenly discover or invented hunter-gatherer societies in 1966. The concept itself goes back centuries. An anthropologist had been studying hunting and gathering populations long before that conference. A.R. Radcliffe Brown published the Andaman Islanders in 1922, based on fieldwork he had conducted between 1906 and 1908. George Murdoch published cross-cultural research on the division of labor between men and women in 1937. Julian Stewart was comparing hunting and gathering societies by the 1930s and continued doing so in his 1955 book Theory of Culture Change. So no, the participants at the 1966 Men the Hunter conference did not invent hunter-gatherer societies or the idea of a division of labor between men and women. And here's what I do not understand. Why can't we not simply acknowledge the importance of what women generally did? Why is hunting automatically treated as the glamorous and important job, while gathering is treated as some irrelevant side activity? Even the research presented in the Men the Hunter volume showed that hunting was often not the main source of food. Outside Arctic and sub-Arctic environments, hunting was estimated to provide only around 20-40% of the diet. Gathering was often more reliable and, in some societies, brought in most of the everyday calories. Hunting supplied meat, fat, and important nutrients, but it could also fail. Both roles were essential. So instead of saying women were also extremely important because gathering kept people alive, they apparently need to prove that women were secretly doing the men's job as well. Why? Women do not need to have done exactly the same things as men for their contribution to matter. Men and women were not competing for the better job title. They were cooperating so that their children and their group would survive. And finally, just use some common sense and critical thinking. Men are, on average, physically larger and stronger. Women become pregnant, give birth, and breastfeed. That doesn't make women incapable of hunting, but it creates different physical costs and practical constraints. Large-game hunting can involve traveling long distances, pursuing animals under dangerous conditions, and performing an activity that cannot always be interrupted because your baby needs to be fed. Gathering tends to produce more predictable returns and, depending on the resource, can be more compatible with child care. That doesn't mean gathering was easy. Women could also travel considerable distances, carry heavy loads, process food, collect water and firewood, build shelters, and perform many other physically demanding jobs. Researchers studying this division of labor, specifically identified child care constraints, together with men's greater average size and strength, as factors giving men a comparative advantage in certain types of hunting. Biology is not the complete explanation for every society, but pretending that biology had absolutely nothing to do with it is ridiculous. So now we have cartoons that paint men in a bad light and promote gender wars? Why? These people were not fighting a gender war. They were trying to survive.
